Fire NOC in India: What Every Business Needs to Know

What a fire NOC is, who needs one, the documents and inspection involved, why applications get rejected, and how ongoing fire compliance works in Maharashtra.

Fire Safety · 5 min read · By the Belabloom team · 24 October 2026

"Fire NOC" is one of the most searched compliance terms in Indian business, and one of the most misunderstood. It can mean the approval a building needs before it is occupied, a licence condition for certain kinds of businesses, or the ongoing certificates that prove fire systems are maintained. This guide explains each, and what it takes to pass an inspection the first time.

Fire services are run by states and city authorities, so thresholds, forms and fees differ from place to place. Use this guide to prepare, and confirm the exact requirements with your local fire authority.

What a fire NOC is

A fire No Objection Certificate is written confirmation from the fire authority that a building, or a business inside it, meets the fire and life safety requirements for its use. Most states base their rules on the National Building Code of India 2016, Part 4 (Fire and Life Safety), which sets requirements by type of occupancy, such as business, assembly, educational or industrial, and by building height. The code treats buildings of 15 metres and above as high-rise, with stricter requirements.

There are three situations in which businesses deal with fire approvals:

  1. Building approvals. A building usually needs fire department clearance when its plans are approved and again before it can be occupied.
  2. Business-specific approvals. Many cities require a fire NOC before issuing licences to certain businesses, such as restaurants, hotels, hospitals, schools, cinemas, malls, factories and warehouses storing hazardous goods.
  3. Ongoing compliance. Some states require periodic certificates showing systems are still maintained. Maharashtra is the clearest example, covered below.

Do tenants need their own fire NOC?

If you lease an office in a building that already has fire approval, you usually don't apply for a new building NOC. But two things still apply to you:

  • Your fit-out must not compromise the building's fire systems. Partitions that block sprinklers, false ceilings that hide detectors, or furniture that narrows an exit can put the whole building out of compliance, and changes like these may need approval.
  • If your business type needs its own fire clearance for a licence, such as an eating house, clinic or training institute, you apply for it in addition to the building's approval.

Documents usually required

The list varies, but applications commonly need:

  • Approved building plans, and drawings showing the fire systems, exits and compartments
  • Proof of ownership or tenancy, and the occupancy certificate for the building
  • Details of installed fire systems, with completion and test certificates from the installer
  • An electrical installation certificate, and a structural stability certificate for older buildings in some cities
  • The application form and fee, usually submitted through the state or city's online portal

The process, step by step

  1. Design the fire systems and escape routes to the applicable code for your occupancy and height.
  2. Install the systems through a qualified agency, then test and commission them.
  3. Apply with the documents and fee.
  4. Inspection by a fire officer, who checks the site against the drawings and the code.
  5. Fix the observations, if any, and request a re-inspection.
  6. Receive the NOC. Some NOCs are valid for a fixed period and must be renewed; check the validity printed on yours.

Why applications get sent back

Most rejections come from a short list of avoidable problems:

  • The site doesn't match the submitted drawings, often because partitions or mezzanines were added later.
  • Exits are locked, blocked or used for storage; refuge areas and staircases hold furniture or files.
  • Fire doors are missing self-closers or are wedged open.
  • Extinguishers are expired, the wrong type for the risk, or not where the layout shows them.
  • Fire pumps are not on automatic mode, or the alarm panel shows faults.
  • Emergency lighting and exit signs don't work on battery.
  • Sprinkler heads or detectors are painted over, blocked or missing after a fit-out.
  • Documents are incomplete or certificates are out of date.

A pre-inspection checklist

  • Walk every escape route and remove anything stored in corridors, staircases and refuge areas.
  • Check every exit door opens easily from the inside without a key.
  • Check extinguisher tags, pressure gauges and seals, and that each one is mounted and visible.
  • Test the alarm panel and clear faults; trigger a sample of detectors and call points.
  • Run the fire pumps and confirm they are on automatic.
  • Switch off mains power to a section and confirm emergency lights and exit signs stay lit.
  • Compare the site against the drawings and update either the site or the drawings.
  • Put all certificates, test reports and service records in one file.

Ongoing compliance in Maharashtra

Under the Maharashtra Fire Prevention and Life Safety Measures Act, 2006, owners and occupiers must keep fire prevention and life safety measures in good working order. Twice a year, in January and July, they must submit a certificate in Form B, issued by a licensed agency, to the Chief Fire Officer, confirming the systems are maintained. Missing it is one of the most common compliance gaps we find in audits.

Whatever state you are in, the same habits keep you compliant between inspections: regular extinguisher servicing as set out in IS 2190, scheduled testing of alarms and pumps, periodic evacuation drills, staff trained as fire wardens, and a single file of up-to-date records.
